summaries.example: Imagine two statements: “The school bell is ringing” and “A triangle has three sides.” The first may be true now but could have been different. The second is true by its meaning. Modal logic gives us tools for talking about differences like these: what is possible, what must be true, and what cannot be true.
summaries.summary: Modal logic is the study of necessity and possibility. In a broad sense, it can also study other ways of speaking about truth, such as what is known, required, or always happening. The entry mainly follows the modern history of the narrower subject: the logic of what must be true and what might be true. C.I. Lewis began an important syntactic tradition in the early twentieth century. He wanted a better way to represent strict implication, meaning that one statement really follows from another, rather than merely being connected by an ordinary truth rule. Lewis and later logicians created several systems, named S1 through S5, with different rules. Logicians also used matrices, which are organized collections of values, to test systems and study whether rules could be proved independently. Later, Rudolf Carnap and Saul Kripke developed semantic approaches. These approaches explain modal claims using descriptions or structures of possible worlds. Kripke’s work connected worlds with accessibility relations and helped establish completeness and decidability results for several systems. The history shows that modal logic grew through both mathematical techniques and philosophical questions about possibility and necessity.
key_ideas: Modal logic studies necessity and possibility. Related forms study knowledge, duties, or time.
C.I. Lewis developed several early systems of modal logic after worrying that ordinary implication did not capture every idea of logical inference.
The systems S1 through S5 differ in strength: stronger systems prove everything weaker systems prove, plus more.
Later work used models and possible worlds to explain modal operators and to prove results about systems.
Different systems can be useful because people may disagree about which rules best express necessity or implication.
summaries.why_it_matters: Modal language appears in everyday reasoning: we ask what could happen, what must happen, and what cannot happen. Modal logic gives these ideas precise rules. It also shows how mathematics and philosophy can work together. A small change in an axiom can create a different logical system, so studying the systems helps us understand what our words about possibility and necessity really mean.

important_terms.definition: A kind of logic that studies ways something can be true, such as being possible or necessary.
A word or symbol that changes how we think about a statement, for example “possibly” or “necessarily.”
A statement that must be true, or could not be false, in the intended way of thinking.
A statement that could be true, even if it is not true right now.
A formal rule system containing starting rules, called axioms, and rules for drawing conclusions.

questions_to_think_about: Is something true now always necessary? Why or why not?
What might a “possible world” mean if it is not a planet?
Should an impossible statement be allowed to imply any statement?
Why might logicians want more than one system of modal logic?

summaries.example: Suppose a security system records whether a door is open in different situations. In one formal model, a world is a situation, and an accessibility relation tells us which situations count as alternatives to a given one. “Necessarily, the door is locked” is true at a world when the door is locked at every accessible alternative; “possibly, the door is locked” is true when it is locked at at least one accessible alternative. Changing the properties of accessibility changes the modal logic. For example, adding transitivity corresponds to axiom 4 and is characteristic of S4-style semantics, while adding symmetry helps characterize system B.
summaries.summary: The entry traces the modern development of modal logic from C.I. Lewis’s early syntactic work to Carnap’s and Kripke’s semantic approaches. Modal logic can be understood broadly as the logic of modalities—different ways a statement may be true—but the historical focus here is alethic modality: necessity and possibility. The syntactic tradition began with Lewis’s criticism of material implication. Classical propositional logic validates formulas in which a false proposition implies anything and a true proposition is implied by anything. Lewis accepted these results under the truth-functional reading but argued that they do not capture implication understood as logical inference. His systems of strict implication, S1 through S5, differ in axioms and rules. They are not all equally strong or mutually comparable, and debates about the proper principles of deduction led to further systems and alternative axiomatizations. Gödel’s treatment of S4, followed by work by Feys, von Wright, and Lemmon, made the separation between a propositional calculus and modal principles especially clear. The distinction between normal systems—those containing axiom K and necessitation—and non-normal systems became important. Algebraic and matrix methods provided ways to test consistency, independence, modality counts, decidability, and representation. The entry then turns to semantics. Carnap used state-descriptions to formalize logical truth and interpreted necessity through analyticity, but his maximal validity notion caused problems for quantified modal logic. Kripke’s possible-worlds semantics introduced a more general notion of validity, worlds as evaluation points, and an accessibility relation. key_ideas: The entry distinguishes a broad use of “modal logic” for many modalities from the stricter traditional use focused on alethic necessity and possibility.
Lewis’s syntactic project began with dissatisfaction about material implication: some classically valid formulas did not match the intended idea of implication as logical consequence.

Lewis proposed several systems. S1 is weaker than S2, S3, S4, and S5 in the sense that stronger systems contain the theorems of weaker ones, though some systems are not simply ordered in every comparison.

Gödel, Feys, von Wright, and Lemmon helped reorganize modal systems by separating a propositional base from specifically modal axioms and rules. Normal systems include propositional calculus, axiom K, and necessitation; K is the smallest normal system, while T, B, S4, and S5 add further principles.

Matrices and algebraic methods were used to investigate consistency, independence, numbers of modalities, decidability, and representation. Dugundji showed that S1–S5 do not have finite characteristic matrices, while McKinsey established decidability results for S2 and S4.

Carnap’s state-descriptions anticipated possible-worlds semantics but used a maximal notion of validity that created difficulties, especially for quantified S5. Kripke’s semantics allowed arbitrary collections of worlds and introduced accessibility relations, supporting completeness and decidability results for several systems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Modal logic makes precise distinctions that ordinary language often leaves vague: what is true, what must be true, and what could be true. Its history also illustrates a central lesson about formal philosophy: changing a rule or axiom changes the consequences of a system, so the choice of system depends partly on the intended interpretation. The development from Lewis’s syntax through algebraic methods and Kripke’s semantics shows how proof theory, mathematics, and philosophical interpretation can illuminate one another. important_terms.definition: The branch of modal logic concerned specifically with necessity and possibility, rather than knowledge, obligation, or time.
An intensified, non-truth-functional conditional intended to express that one proposition follows from another in a strict logical sense.
A formal sentence accepted as a starting principle in a logical system.
A rule allowing a proven formula to be prefixed with necessity; in symbols, if α is provable, then □α is provable.
A formal structure used to evaluate formulas, consisting of values, designated values, and operations for logical connectives.
A semantic structure with worlds or indices and a relation indicating which worlds are relevant or accessible from which others.
The result that every formula provable in a system is valid in its semantics, and, conversely, every semantically valid formula is provable.
The property that there is an effective method for determining whether a formula is a theorem of a system.

summaries.example: Think about a school play. It may be possible for the play to happen outdoors, but it is necessary that the actors follow the script’s agreed rules for the performance. A modal logician might represent these different claims with operators such as “possibly” and “necessarily.” The answer can change if we consider different alternative situations, such as different weather or different rules for deciding which situations count as relevant.
summaries.summary: Modal logic studies statements about different ways of being true. In its broadest use, it can concern necessity and possibility, knowledge, duties, or time. The entry uses the narrower traditional meaning: the logic of what must be true and what could be true. Its story begins with C.I. Lewis, who questioned whether the ordinary truth-based conditional captured the everyday idea of implication. In classical logic, certain formulas allow a false statement to imply any statement, or allow any statement to imply a true one. Lewis did not say these results were mathematically wrong under material implication. He argued that they did not match implication understood as a genuine relation of logical consequence. He therefore developed systems of strict implication. The best-known systems are S1 through S5. They differ in their axioms and rules, and they are generally arranged from weaker to stronger, although not every pair is simply comparable. Other logicians proposed alternative systems and ways of presenting them. Gödel’s work helped show how a propositional foundation could be kept separate from modal rules. This led to the study of normal systems, including K, T, B, S4, and S5, and to clearer comparisons among them. Researchers also used matrices and algebraic methods. These methods could show that formulas were independent, test consistency, count different modal forms, and sometimes establish decidability. The semantic tradition began with Carnap’s state-descriptions, which were influenced by the idea of possible situations. Carnap tried to connect necessity with logical truth or analyticity, but his version of validity had difficulties, particularly for quantified systems. key_ideas: “Modal logic” can be used broadly for logic about necessity, knowledge, obligation, or time, but this entry mainly studies necessity and possibility.
Lewis challenged the idea that ordinary material implication fully captures the meaning of “implies” in reasoning and proof.
The systems S1–S5 show that logicians can build several systems with different strengths. A stronger system proves everything a weaker system proves, but some systems are not neatly comparable.
Later axiomatizations separated ordinary propositional logic from modal principles. Normal systems include axiom K and necessitation; T, B, S4, and S5 add different principles.
Matrices and algebraic structures helped researchers study consistency, independence, the number of distinct modal patterns, and decision procedures.
Carnap and Kripke developed semantic methods. Kripke’s possible-worlds approach used worlds, accessibility, and a broad notion of validity to obtain important completeness and decidability results.
summaries.why_it_matters: Modal logic helps us examine familiar words such as “must,” “may,” and “could” with exact rules. It also explains why disagreement about one principle can produce different systems. The historical development matters because it connects philosophical questions about necessity with mathematical questions about proofs, models, matrices, completeness, and decidability. Studying the subject also shows that a model is not automatically a final philosophical answer: logicians still have to ask what worlds, accessibility, and necessity are supposed to represent.

important_terms.definition: Logic about ways a statement may be true, especially whether it is necessary or possible.
A statement or symbol that adds a meaning such as “possibly” or “necessarily.”
A meaning of implication according to which the conclusion genuinely follows from the premise, not merely because of their truth values.
A formal system’s basic accepted principle, used with rules to derive further formulas.
A rule saying that if a formula is provable, then its necessity is also provable in systems that contain this rule.
A mathematical tool with values and operations used to test whether formulas and rules work in a logical system.
A model containing possible situations, often called worlds, together with information about which situations are accessible from each one.

questions_to_think_about: Can a statement be true without being necessary? Give an example.
Why might a logician reject the idea that a false statement automatically implies every statement?
What could make one possible world accessible from another?
Why would researchers want several logical systems instead of one?
How might changing the rules for possible worlds change what counts as valid?
